text.p: Following are key facts about India, which completes 50 years of independence from British colonial rule on August 15:
POPULATION: 936 million (source: Planning Ministry). About 75 percent live in rural areas (source: 1991 Census). Registered voters 590 million (source: Election Commission estimate, 1996).
Religions: Hindus (82 percent), Moslems (12 percent), Christians (2.3 percent), Sikhs (2.0 percent), Buddhists (0.8 percent), Jains (0.4 percent). (Source: 1991 census)
Official language: Hindi in the Devanagari script. Regional languages are widely used, as well as English.
Literacy: 52 percent (source: 1991 census).

AREA: 1.3 million sq miles (3.3 million sq km) stretching from the Himalayas in the north to the Indian ocean in the south. India shares borders with Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Burma and Bangladesh.
CAPITAL: New Delhi.
ARMED FORCES: (Source: Institute of Strategic Studies, 1995)
Total strength in 1995 -- 1.15 million men plus 535,000 reserves.
Army -- 980,000, 3,500 tanks, 1,507 armoured fighting/ personnel carriers.
Air Force -- 110,000 men; 799 combat aircraft including Jaguars, MiG-21s, MiG-23s, MiG-27s, MiG-29s, Sukhoi Su-30Ks and Mirage-2000s, 36 armed helicopters.

Navy -- 55,000 men, 26 principal surface combatants with two aircraft carriers, five destroyers and 19 frigates. It also has 18 corvettes, eight missile craft, 19 submarines, seven patrol offshore, 11 patrol inshore. Naval Air Force has 68 combat aircraft, including 20 Sea Harriers.

ECONOMY: Annual per capita income in 1994 was $320 (source: World Bank, 1996). Some 36 percent live below the poverty line, unable to afford minimum adequate nutrition and non-food essentials (source: Planning Ministry).
Agriculture is the main occupation for around 70 percent of the population.
There is substantial industry in urban areas, including aircraft, ships, railway rolling stock, passenger and commercial vehicles, textiles, atomic energy, electronics and gem cutting.
Labour force: 314 million, with 36.7 million registered at government employment bureaux for jobs (Census, 1991).
Annual GDP growth rate: 6.8 percent in 1996/97, compared to 7.1 percent in 1995/96 (Source: Planning Ministry).
Main exports: Gems, jewellery, ready-made garments, cotton yarn and fabrics, handicrafts, cereals, marine products, transport equipment.
Main imports: Crude, petroleum products, chemicals, machinery, electrical machinery, fertilisers, iron, steel, pearls, precious and semi-precious stones.
Total external debt: $92.20 billion at end-March 1997, compared with $92.6 billion at end-March 1996 (Finance Ministry).

MODERN HISTORY: India, which traces its civilisation back 5,000 years, won independence from Britain in 1947 in a welter of sectarian bloodshed as the subcontinent was partitioned into secular but predominantly Hindu India and Moslem Pakistan.
India has fought three wars with Pakistan, two over Kashmir. In 1962, India also fought a short border war with China.
India is a leading member of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) and the Commonwealth. During the Cold War it had close relations with the Soviet Union, which was a major arms supplier.
Since the breakup of the Soviet Union, India and the United States have strengthened ties, particularly business relations, but Delhi remains close to Moscow.
India exploded an atomic bomb in 1974 but says it has not built any nuclear weapons.
India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, apostle of neutralism and a founder of NAM, died in 1964. Two years later his daughter, Indira Gandhi, became prime minister.

Mrs Gandhi imposed a 1975-77 State of Emergency during which hundreds of thousands of political opponents were imprisoned and the press censored. She was defeated in elections in 1977 but returned to power in 1980.

She was assassinated by Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984, in retaliation for dispatching troops into Amritsar's Golden Temple, Sikhdom's holiest shrine. More than 1,000 people were killed in the June 1984 operation to oust separatist militants using the temple as a headquarters.
Her son Rajiv Gandhi took over as prime minister with India in turmoil as Hindus killed some 2,700 Sikhs in revenge.

Two months later Rajiv Gandhi led Congress to a landslide election win. He pledged to modernise India's regulation-bound economy but achieved little in concrete terms, although he set the tone for later sweeping reforms.
He lost power in a November 1989 election. Two centre-left governments followed but fell in quick succession, plagued by internal divisions. Polls were called for May 1991.
On May 21, 1991, with one day's voting completed, Gandhi was killed by a woman suicide bomber while campaigning in the southern state of Tamil Nadu.
India blamed Tamil Tigers fighting for independence in Sri Lanka, against whom Gandhi had sent Indian troops. The Tigers denied all responsibility.

P.V. Narasimha Rao, who introduced sweeping economic reforms after he became the Prime Minister in 1991, led the Congress party to its worst ever electoral defeat in the 1996 elections as many of his colleagues got enmeshed in corruption scandals.

In April-May 1996, elections threw up a fractured mandate and the Hindu Nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party emerged as the single largest party with 161 seats out of a total of 545, but well short of an outright majority in the house.

The party president Atal Bihari Vajpayee had to relinquish power after a short stint of 12 days in the prime minister's office as his party failed to muster the required numbers to prove its majority on the floor of the house.
On June 1, 1996, a 13 member coalition of centre and leftist parties came to power with H.D.Deve Gowda as the prime minister.

The 140-member Congress party withdrew its crucial make-or-break support to the United Front in March 1997, leading to the fall of Deve Gowda's government in April. The coalition then changed its leader to win back Congress support and formed a new government under Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral.
The parliamentary elections of May 1996 were the first in troubled northern Jammu and Kashmir state since an Islamic separatist insurgency erupted in January 1990.
More than 20,000 people have died in the violence involving Moslem guerrillas fighting for independence or merger with Pakistan.
State chief minister Farooq Abdullah of the National Conference Party, who took office on October 9, 1996 after almost seven years of federal rule, put the toll near 50,000.
In December 1992 Hindu zealots tore down a 16th century mosque in the northern town of Ayodhya, sparking nationwide riots in which some 3,000 people, mostly Moslems, died.
Many Hindus believed it was located at the birthplace of the deity Lord Ram.
India has a two-chamber parliamentary system of government. The head of state is an indirectly elected president with mainly ceremonial powers except in political crises.
India's 25 states elect their own assemblies, but Delhi has the power to impose central rule, as it did in Punjab in 1987 and in Jammu and Kashmir in 1990 to curb separatist movements.
